This vignette shows a first analysis with fasttrop. You make a practice
panel, you calculate the TROP estimate, and you read the result. The article
"TROP in plain words" on the
[package website](https://farach.github.io/fasttrop/) explains the ideas of the
method.

## The data

fasttrop uses panel data in long format. Each row is one unit in one period.
The data must have four columns:

- the outcome
- the treatment indicator, with the values 0 and 1
- the unit identifier
- the period identifier

The function `trop_simulate()` makes a practice panel with a known effect. In
this panel, 5 of 20 units get the treatment in the last 3 of 12 periods. The
true effect is 1 for each treated cell.

```{r}
library(fasttrop)
panel <- trop_simulate(n_units = 20, n_periods = 12, n_treated = 5, n_post = 3,
                       effect = 1, seed = 1)
head(panel)
```

The column `y` is the outcome, and the column `d` is the treatment indicator.
The column `y0` is the outcome without the treatment. Real data does not have
this column. The practice panel has it, so you can compare the estimate with
the truth.

## A first estimate

To calculate the estimate, give `trop()` the data and the names of the four
columns. In this first fit, you set the tuning parameters. This makes the fit
fast.

```{r}
fit <- trop(panel, outcome = "y", treatment = "d", unit = "unit", time = "time",
            lambda = c(time = 0.2, unit = 0.5, nn = 0.5), n_boot = 100, seed = 1)
fit
```

After the title, the output has three lines:

1. The method, the design of the panel, the size of the panel, and the number
   of treated cells.
2. The average treatment effect on the treated (ATT), with the bootstrap
   standard error (SE) and the 95% confidence interval.
3. The tuning parameters.

The true ATT of this panel is 1. The interval contains this value.

## Parts of the result

Use these functions to get parts of the result:

```{r}
coef(fit)
confint(fit)
head(as.data.frame(fit))
```

The function `as.data.frame()` gives the effect for each treated cell. The ATT
is the mean of these effects.

## Let the data select the tuning parameters

TROP has three tuning parameters:

- `time` sets how fast the time weights decrease with the distance from the
  treated period. With 0, all periods get the same weight.
- `unit` sets how fast the unit weights decrease when the outcome history of
  a unit is different from the treated unit. With 0, all units get the same
  weight.
- `nn` is the penalty on the low-rank term. A larger value gives a simpler
  low-rank term. With `Inf`, the model has no low-rank term.

If you do not set `lambda`, cross-validation selects the tuning parameters
from the grid of `trop_grid()`. To make this example fast, the
cross-validation uses a sample of 60 untreated cells.

```{r}
fit_cv <- trop(panel, outcome = "y", treatment = "d", unit = "unit", time = "time",
               cv_cells = 60, n_boot = 100, seed = 1)
summary(fit_cv)
```

The function `summary()` also gives the result of the tuning, the bootstrap,
and the time of the calculation. With `cv_cells = NULL`, the default, the
cross-validation uses all untreated cells, as in the paper. This takes more
time, but it uses all the data.

## The local method and the global method

The default method is the local method of the paper. It calculates a
separate fit for each treated cell. The global method is the method of the
Python package from the authors. It calculates one fit for all treated cells.
You can use the global method only for a block design. In a block design, all
treated units start the treatment in the same period and stay treated.

```{r}
fit_global <- trop(panel, outcome = "y", treatment = "d", unit = "unit",
                   time = "time", method = "global",
                   lambda = c(time = 0.2, unit = 0.5, nn = 0.5), n_boot = 100,
                   seed = 1)
coef(fit_global)
```

## Standard errors and intervals

A unit bootstrap gives the standard error. Each draw takes a sample of units
with replacement and calculates the estimate again. fasttrop keeps the tuning
parameters fixed in each draw. The argument `n_boot` sets the number of draws.
The default is 200 draws.

The default interval is a normal interval. To get a percentile interval, set
`ci = "percentile"`. The bootstrap is correct only with many treated units.
For a panel with fewer than five treated units, fasttrop gives a warning
message.

## Threads and seeds

fasttrop runs its model fits in C, and it can use more than one thread. The
function `trop_threads()` gives the default number of threads. To set the
number of threads, use `trop_control()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fit <- trop(panel, outcome = "y", treatment = "d", unit = "unit", time = "time",
            control = trop_control(threads = 4))
```

The number of threads does not change the results. With the same `seed`, a fit
gives the same result each time. The `seed` argument does not change the
random number generator of your R session.
